title: Chronic Kidney Disease: Stage by eGFR and Albuminuria
bottomLine: CKD is persistent kidney abnormality, not one low eGFR. Risk is determined by both eGFR and albuminuria, and treatment should reduce kidney failure and cardiovascular risk while avoiding nephrotoxins.
recognize: Diabetes and hypertension are common causes; albuminuria can identify high risk even before eGFR is markedly reduced.
differentiate: AKI is an acute change; CKD requires chronicity or established structural markers.
assessment: Review BP, diabetes, NSAIDs, contrast exposure, urinary symptoms, family history and volume status.
workup: Repeat kidney function to establish chronicity, quantify urine ACR and investigate hematuria/structural disease when present.
management: Use BP control, RAAS blockade when indicated, SGLT2 inhibitor and other cardiorenal therapy according to contemporary Canadian guidance; manage anemia/mineral-bone complications at appropriate stage.
medicationSafety: Dose-adjust renally cleared drugs and avoid chronic NSAID use when possible.
A modest creatinine rise after RAAS therapy can be expected, but marked rise or hyperkalemia requires reassessment.
counselling: Discuss sick-day medication plans when dehydration could precipitate AKI.
followUp: Monitor eGFR, ACR, potassium and cardiovascular risk based on stage.
examTrap: Calling a single eGFR of 55 chronic kidney disease without confirming persistence or other markers.
oneLinePearl: CKD prognosis is eGFR plus albuminuria plus trend.

title: Nephritic Syndrome: Hematuria Plus Kidney Inflammation
bottomLine: Hematuria with proteinuria, hypertension, edema and rising creatinine suggests glomerular inflammation and needs urgent cause-directed evaluation, especially when kidney function is deteriorating rapidly.
recognize: Dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts support glomerular bleeding.
differentiate: Urologic hematuria usually lacks RBC casts and significant glomerular proteinuria.
assessment: Ask recent infection, autoimmune symptoms, rash, pulmonary symptoms, medications and systemic vasculitis features.
workup: Use urinalysis/microscopy, ACR/PCR, creatinine, complements and targeted serologies; nephrology may need kidney biopsy.
management: Urgently refer suspected rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis; control BP/volume and treat the underlying immune or infectious cause.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric immunosuppression without appropriate diagnostic and infection evaluation except under specialist emergency direction.
counselling: Explain why blood in urine plus kidney dysfunction differs from a simple bladder infection.
followUp: Track renal function and urine protein closely through nephrology.
examTrap: Treating cola-coloured urine and hypertension as UTI without checking kidney function and urine microscopy.
oneLinePearl: Hematuria plus proteinuria plus rising creatinine is glomerular until proven otherwise.

title: Nephrotic Syndrome: Protein Loss With Thrombosis Risk
bottomLine: Heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia and edema defines nephrotic physiology and carries infection and thrombosis risk. Determine cause and severity rather than treating edema alone.
recognize: Generalized edema, foamy urine, hyperlipidemia and marked proteinuria are typical.
differentiate: Heart failure and cirrhosis can cause edema but do not produce the same glomerular protein-loss pattern.
assessment: Assess diabetes, autoimmune disease, infection, malignancy, medications and thrombosis symptoms.
workup: Quantify urine protein, renal function, albumin, lipids and targeted secondary-cause testing; nephrology may require biopsy.
management: Use sodium/volume management, RAAS and disease-specific treatment; evaluate thrombosis prevention/treatment individually.
medicationSafety: Aggressive diuresis can worsen intravascular depletion despite visible edema.
counselling: Teach VTE and infection warning signs.
followUp: Track proteinuria, albumin, renal function and cause-specific response.
examTrap: Assuming edema means the patient is intravascularly overloaded and giving escalating diuretic without reassessment.
oneLinePearl: Nephrotic patients can be swollen outside and underfilled inside.

title: Hematuria: Glomerular, Stone, Infection, or Cancer?
bottomLine: Visible or persistent microscopic hematuria needs a source. Infection, stones, glomerular disease and urinary malignancy are distinguished by symptoms, urine findings and age/risk—not by repeatedly treating empiric UTI.
recognize: Gross painless hematuria in an older smoker is a malignancy red flag.
Colicky flank pain suggests stone; dysuria/pyuria suggests infection; protein/casts suggest glomerular disease.
differentiate: Menstrual contamination and exercise can cause transient findings but persistent true hematuria still needs evaluation.
assessment: Ask pain, urinary symptoms, smoking, anticoagulants, exercise, trauma, menses and systemic renal symptoms.
workup: Repeat clean urinalysis when contamination is plausible, culture when infection suspected, quantify protein and use risk-based imaging/cystoscopy.
management: Treat the diagnosed cause and refer urologic or nephrologic pathways based on pattern.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulation may reveal bleeding but does not explain away an underlying lesion.
counselling: Explain that blood in urine should not be normalized because a patient is taking anticoagulants.
followUp: Confirm resolution after UTI treatment; persistent hematuria still requires evaluation.
examTrap: Attributing gross hematuria to warfarin and skipping malignancy workup.
oneLinePearl: Anticoagulants uncover hematuria; they do not automatically explain its source.

title: Renal Colic: Stone or Infected Obstruction?
bottomLine: Uncomplicated renal colic can be managed symptomatically, but fever/sepsis with an obstructed urinary system is a urologic emergency requiring drainage plus antimicrobials—not outpatient stone passage.
recognize: Acute colicky flank pain radiating to groin with hematuria is typical.
differentiate: Pyelonephritis, AAA, ectopic pregnancy and ovarian/testicular emergencies can mimic flank/abdominal pain.
assessment: Assess fever, vitals, pregnancy, single kidney, urinary output, prior stones and analgesic contraindications.
workup: Use urinalysis, renal function and imaging matched to pregnancy/radiation considerations and severity.
management: Provide analgesia/hydration to euvolemia and selective medical expulsive therapy; infected obstruction or threatened renal function needs urgent urology.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs are effective for renal colic but may be inappropriate in pregnancy, AKI or high GI risk.
counselling: Stone analysis and recurrence-prevention advice depend on stone risk/history.
followUp: Confirm passage or resolution when obstruction risk persists.
examTrap: Giving antibiotics and sending home a febrile patient with an obstructing stone.
oneLinePearl: Infected obstruction needs drainage, not antibiotics alone.

title: BPH: Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms Need a Differential
bottomLine: Male lower urinary tract symptoms are not automatically BPH. Evaluate infection, medication effects, overactive bladder, neurologic disease, retention and prostate cancer features before treatment.
recognize: Weak stream, hesitancy, intermittency, incomplete emptying and nocturia are common.
differentiate: Irritative symptoms can arise from OAB, UTI or diabetes; red-flag hematuria or abnormal prostate findings require another pathway.
assessment: Use symptom severity, medication review, abdominal/genital exam and prostate assessment when appropriate.
workup: Urinalysis is routine; PSA testing is a shared decision based on cancer-screening context and whether the result would change management.
management: Use lifestyle measures, alpha blockers for rapid symptom relief and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors for appropriate enlarged-prostate phenotypes; surgery/urology for complications or refractory symptoms.
medicationSafety: Alpha blockers can cause orthostatic hypotension; PDE5 inhibitor combinations require BP awareness.
counselling: Discuss sexual adverse effects and realistic onset of benefit.
followUp: Reassess symptoms, retention risk and medication effects.
examTrap: Starting BPH medication in a patient with dysuria and pyuria without evaluating infection.
oneLinePearl: LUTS describes symptoms; BPH is only one cause.

title: Prostatitis: Acute Bacterial Disease Can Become Sepsis
bottomLine: Fever, dysuria, pelvic/perineal pain and a tender prostate suggest acute bacterial prostatitis. Avoid vigorous prostatic massage because bacteremia can worsen; severe illness, retention or abscess concern needs urgent care.
recognize: Systemic symptoms and urinary infection distinguish acute bacterial prostatitis from many chronic pelvic pain syndromes.
differentiate: Pyelonephritis causes flank/CVA symptoms; epididymitis and STI syndromes may coexist or mimic.
assessment: Assess sepsis, retention, STI risk, instrumentation and immunocompromise.
workup: Obtain urinalysis/culture and blood cultures when systemically ill; image when abscess or obstruction is suspected.
management: Use antibiotics with adequate prostatic penetration guided by local resistance/culture; admit severe sepsis, retention or inability to tolerate oral therapy.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary fluoroquinolone use when safer effective options exist and follow local antibiogram guidance.
counselling: Complete therapy and seek care for worsening fever or retention.
followUp: Ensure culture results and symptom resolution; persistent symptoms require reassessment.
examTrap: Performing vigorous prostate massage in acute febrile prostatitis.
oneLinePearl: A hot tender prostate is not a massage diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Urological Association and Canadian antimicrobial stewardship principles

title: Acute Urinary Retention: Decompress and Find the Cause
bottomLine: Painful inability to void with bladder distension requires prompt decompression and cause assessment. Neurologic deficits, infection, medications and outlet obstruction can all cause retention.
recognize: Suprapubic pain/distension and little/no urine output are typical.
differentiate: Anuria from renal failure can be mistaken for retention; bladder scan helps distinguish them.
assessment: Review BPH, constipation, pelvic surgery, anticholinergics/opioids, neurologic symptoms and infection.
workup: Use bladder scan/catheter output, urinalysis and renal function; image/neurologic workup if obstruction or cauda equina is suspected.
management: Catheterize unless contraindicated, treat cause and arrange voiding trial/urology follow-up.
medicationSafety: Anticholinergics, opioids, antihistamines and decongestants can precipitate retention.
counselling: Explain catheter care and medication contributors.
followUp: Do not leave an indwelling catheter without a removal/assessment plan.
examTrap: Giving more oral fluids to a patient with a painfully distended bladder who cannot void.
oneLinePearl: Retention is a plumbing problem first: decompress, then diagnose.

title: Urinary Incontinence: Stress, Urge, Overflow, or Functional?
bottomLine: Incontinence is a symptom with different mechanisms. Identify reversible causes and classify stress, urgency, overflow or functional patterns before choosing therapy.
recognize: Stress leakage occurs with cough/exertion; urgency has sudden compelling need; overflow suggests incomplete emptying; functional incontinence reflects mobility/cognitive/environmental barriers.
differentiate: New incontinence with dysuria may be infection; new retention/weakness may be neurologic emergency.
assessment: Use bladder diary, obstetric/pelvic history, medications, constipation, cognition, mobility and pelvic exam when indicated.
workup: Urinalysis is common; postvoid residual is important when retention/overflow is plausible.
management: Use pelvic-floor therapy for stress symptoms, bladder training for urgency, treat reversible causes and choose medication/surgery selectively.
medicationSafety: Antimuscarinics can worsen cognitive impairment, dry mouth, constipation and retention; consider anticholinergic burden.
counselling: Normalize discussion and reduce stigma; continence products can be part of supportive care while causes are treated.
followUp: Reassess symptom burden and medication harms.
examTrap: Starting an antimuscarinic without checking postvoid residual in suspected overflow incontinence.
oneLinePearl: Classify the leak before you medicate the bladder.

title: Erectile Dysfunction: A Vascular Symptom Until Proven Otherwise
bottomLine: Erectile dysfunction often reflects vascular, endocrine, medication or psychogenic factors and can precede overt cardiovascular disease. Evaluate risk before prescribing.
recognize: Diabetes, smoking, hypertension, vascular disease, depression and many medications contribute.
differentiate: Situational preserved morning erections may suggest psychogenic contribution, but mixed causes are common.
assessment: Assess onset, libido, erections, relationship context, cardiovascular symptoms, medications/substances and endocrine symptoms.
workup: Screen cardiometabolic risk; testosterone testing is indicated when low libido or hypogonadism features are present, not universally.
management: Treat cardiovascular risk and underlying causes; PDE5 inhibitors are first-line for many patients when safe.
medicationSafety: PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated with nitrates and require caution with hypotension/alpha blockers.
counselling: Use nonjudgmental sexual history and include partner concerns when the patient wishes.
followUp: Reassess efficacy, side effects and underlying risk factors.
examTrap: Prescribing sildenafil without asking about nitrate use.
oneLinePearl: ED can be an early vascular warning sign.
sourceBasis: Canadian Urological Association erectile dysfunction guideline

title: Dialysis Patient Deterioration: Access, Potassium, Volume, Infection
bottomLine: In a dialysis patient, dyspnea, weakness, fever or hypotension should trigger immediate consideration of hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, access infection, sepsis and dialysis-related volume issues.
recognize: Missed dialysis can produce hyperkalemia, acidosis and volume overload; catheter access increases bloodstream-infection risk.
differentiate: Intradialytic hypotension can be volume-related, but persistent hypotension/fever requires evaluation for sepsis or cardiac disease.
assessment: Ask last dialysis, dry weight, missed sessions, access type, fever/chills and medication changes; inspect access without using it outside trained protocol.
workup: Obtain ECG, potassium, chemistry and cultures when infection suspected; chest imaging as indicated.
management: Treat life-threatening hyperkalemia/pulmonary edema/sepsis immediately and contact nephrology for urgent dialysis indications.
medicationSafety: Many drugs require post-dialysis timing or dose adjustment; avoid assuming standard renal dosing applies.
counselling: Address transportation/access barriers behind missed dialysis rather than labelling nonadherence.
followUp: Coordinate with the dialysis unit before changing chronic medications.
examTrap: Treating dyspnea as pneumonia without checking missed dialysis and volume status.
oneLinePearl: In dialysis, always ask: potassium, volume, access, infection, last treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian nephrology and dialysis practice resources

title: Proteinuria: Confirm, Quantify, Risk-Stratify
bottomLine: Dipstick protein is a screening clue. Confirm persistent albumin/protein loss quantitatively, determine whether it is transient or glomerular and use the result to stratify kidney and cardiovascular risk.
recognize: Fever, exercise and orthostatic states can cause transient proteinuria; persistent albuminuria is common in diabetes/hypertension.
differentiate: Albumin-predominant glomerular disease differs from light-chain proteinuria, which may be missed by standard albumin-focused testing.
assessment: Assess diabetes, BP, edema, hematuria, systemic disease, medications and family history.
workup: Use urine ACR/PCR, repeat testing to confirm persistence and renal function; investigate nephritic/nephrotic features when present.
management: Treat the underlying cause and use kidney-protective therapy according to CKD risk category.
medicationSafety: RAAS and SGLT2 therapies require potassium/renal monitoring and pregnancy considerations.
counselling: Explain that urine protein is both a kidney marker and cardiovascular risk marker.
followUp: Trend ACR/PCR after treatment and according to CKD risk.
examTrap: Referring to a single positive dipstick as established chronic proteinuric kidney disease.
oneLinePearl: Confirm the protein, quantify it, then interpret it with eGFR and urine sediment.
